originalTitle: The ban on robot vacuums won’t make them safer, only worse

content: No other gadget knows as much about your home as a robot vacuum. They map your space, learn your routines, and many now carry a camera and microphone into every room in your house. As AI gives them a better understanding of what they see, the privacy and security risks these autonomous robots pose are only growing. That’s why greater scrutiny makes sense, but the ban on foreign-made mobile robots issued by the Federal Communications Commission earlier this week — implemented to address “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons” — doesn’t actually judge products by how secure they are, just where they’re built. It effectively means no new robot vacuums from major companies can enter the US market unless they are built here. And spoiler alert: none are. Cybersecurity and manufacturing are not the same thing. If the goal is safer robot vacuums (and robot lawnmowers, companion bots, humanoids, and all the other robots this ban sweeps up), this policy misses the mark. A meaningful security standard for robots would require encrypted map storage, security audits, vulnerability disclosures, and clear data retention policies. Instead, this ban means Americans will see fewer new models, slower innovation, and more expensive robot vacuums. In short, we’ll get worse vacuums than those we have today. [Image: The Matic robot vacuum is the only model currently assembled in the US, but it doesn’t use enough US-made parts to be considered American made. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2025/10/258028_Matic_Robot_Vacuum_JTuohy_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I’ve been covering and testing robot vacuums for over a decade, and have seen dozens of privacy and security stories. The fear that your robot vacuum could spy on you or leak your data isn’t paranoia; it’s a well-documented fact that we have personal experience with here at The Verge. Many of the industry’s largest manufacturers — including Dreame, Ecovacs, Roborock, iRobot, and Shark — have suffered security vulnerabilities or data breaches. Those failures don’t point toward regulating manufacturing, but toward the need for stronger cybersecurity requirements, like those defined by the government’s Cyber Trust Mark program. But that program doesn’t exist yet, and if it ever does, it will be entirely voluntary. This manufacturing ban applies to any foreign-made robot, but footnotes in the FCC’s public notice indicate that China is a particular concern, warning that foreign governments could use vulnerabilities found in advanced robotics to access sensitive data. China’s commerce ministry has already called the policy “discriminatory and suppressive against Chinese companies and products.” There are real security advantages to domestic robot production. Mehul Nariyawala, president and co-founder of Matic, the only robot vacuum currently assembled in the US (although with too many foreign parts to be considered US-made), points out that domestic manufacturing makes it easier to ensure there are no hardware backdoors and to hold companies accountable for any failures. But a robot vacuum made in Massachusetts isn’t automatically more secure than one made in Shenzhen. And the FCC’s ban doesn’t actually take steps to ensure they will be. The robot ban is a carbon copy of those the FCC has issued to Wi-Fi routers and drones over the last few months. So far, it has already granted several waivers to router companies that don’t appear to be moving their manufacturing to the US, which the waivers require. This raises questions about how consistently and fairly the new rules will be enforced and whether they can actually achieve their intended effect. Today, the practical consequences won’t be better security — the millions of robot vacuums already in American homes remain unaffected, as do any currently sold models. If these really are a risk, and we’ve seen plenty of evidence they can be, why leave the largest source of that risk exactly where it is?  In an optimistic future, the ban could spur American manufacturing. Nariyawala believes it “creates the conditions for American startups to design, engineer, and build all manner of trustworthy robots at scale.” He adds that consumer robots are where robotics manufacturing reaches scale, and the supply chains they require are the same ones defense, industrial, and healthcare robots will depend on. “Get it right, educate customers to demand it, and that domestic supply chain stops being an aspiration and becomes an industry,” he says. But even if he’s right, and he has more incentive than most to hope he is, that transition will take years. Today’s Matic relies heavily on imported parts, and its price is going up to $1,495 in September, showing how far building these products in the US is from replacing the $300 robot vacuum you can buy at Walmart. Meanwhile, restricting the import of new products means US households will miss out on the next wave of innovations in a fast-moving category. [Image: This was iRobot’s first combination mopping robot, which arrived in 2022. iRobot’s reluctance to adopt lidar and to offer mopping on its robot vacuums hurt it, leading to the company being swallowed up by its Chinese competition. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/24241350/226425_Roomba_Combo_Review_JTuohy_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Chinese manufacturers may have started out as fast followers, but they have transformed the robot vacuum industry over the past decade. Fierce competition brought better navigation, improved obstacle avoidance, self-emptying docks, and much better mopping systems. chineseTitle: 对扫地机器人的禁令不会让它们变得更安全，只会变得更糟

chineseContent: 没有任何其他小工具比扫地机器人更了解您的家。他们绘制你的空间地图，了解你的日常生活习惯，现在许多人都带着相机和麦克风进入你家的每个房间。随着人工智能让他们更好地理解他们所看到的东西，这些自主机器人带来的隐私和安全风险只会越来越大。这就是为什么更严格的审查是有道理的，但美国联邦通信委员会本周早些时候发布的针对外国制造的移动机器人的禁令——旨在解决“美国国家安全或美国人的安全和保障面临的不可接受的风险”——实际上并没有根据产品的安全程度来判断产品，而只是根据它们的制造地点来判断。这实际上意味着大公司的新机器人吸尘器不能进入美国市场，除非它们是在美国制造的。剧透警告：没有。网络安全和制造业不是一回事。如果目标是更安全的机器人吸尘器（以及机器人割草机、伴侣机器人、人形机器人以及该禁令所涵盖的所有其他机器人），那么这项政策就没有达到目的。有意义的机器人安全标准需要加密地图存储、安全审计、漏洞披露和明确的数据保留策略。相反，这项禁令意味着美国人将看到更少的新型号、更慢的创新以及更昂贵的机器人吸尘器。简而言之，我们会得到比现在更糟糕的吸尘器。 [图片：Matic 扫地机器人是目前在美国组装的唯一型号，但它没有使用足够多的美国制造零部件，因此不能被视为美国制造。 https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2025/10/258028_Matic_Robot_Vacuum_JTuohy_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] 十多年来，我一直在报道和测试机器人吸尘器，并且看到了数十个隐私和安全故事。的f
